oil.summary: Crude surged to its strongest weekly gain in months — WTI +13.4% on the week to $80.97/bbl, Brent +14.3% to $86.89 — as the US-Iran conflict escalated sharply. A US missile strike on an oil tanker to enforce the Iran naval blockade, expanded sanctions targeting the Shamkhani network, and Iran's vow to maintain the blockade until attacks cease all drove rapid rebuilding of a geopolitical risk premium. Front-month product cracks diverged: RBOB fell 3.3% on the day and Heating Oil dropped 1.75%, suggesting some demand-side anxiety even as crude held firm. China's decision to hike retail gasoline and diesel prices effective July 18 reflects the pass-through of the weekly surge, while India and South Africa moving to boost strategic petroleum reserves signals defensive positioning. IEA members had already agreed to a record 400 mb release earlier this year, providing a partial buffer against price spiraling further.
drivers: US missile strike on oil tanker and tightening naval blockade of Iran driving sharp geopolitical risk premium into crude
Strait of Hormuz closure persisting since March; South Korea rerouting via Red Sea, Iraq planning Syria/Turkey pipeline alternatives
China retail fuel price hike effective July 18; India and South Africa accelerating strategic reserve builds amid supply uncertainty

gas.summary: TTF natural gas rocketed +15.7% on the week to €56.31/MWh and is up nearly 35% over the past month, overwhelmingly driven by Hormuz disruption cascading into European LNG supply chains. Pakistan is actively seeking spot LNG cargoes for July-August delivery after Hormuz traffic halted, while China's state importers are urgently negotiating long-term LNG supply contracts with non-Hormuz-dependent exporters — a structural shift that could tighten Atlantic and Pacific Basin cargoes simultaneously. Iran-linked LPG tankers executing U-turns under the US blockade add further noise to near-term supply. Henry Hub, by contrast, is largely insulated from these dynamics, slipping 1.3% on the week and down over 10% on the month. JERA's exploration of a US IPO is a longer-term corporate development with no immediate price implication.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz closure squeezing LNG flows from the Gulf, pushing TTF to a +35% one-month rally
Pakistan and China scrambling for spot and long-term LNG alternatives to Hormuz-dependent suppliers
Henry Hub decoupled from geopolitical LNG stress, continuing its month-long softening trend on domestic fundamentals

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up 1.25% on the day to $75.71/EUA but remain largely range-bound on the week (+0.87%) and month (+0.44%), suggesting the carbon market has not yet priced a sustained fossil fuel demand shock from the Hormuz crisis. The dominant input cost driver for European power generators remains TTF, which is up 35% in a month, compressing spark spreads and elevating gas-to-power costs across the continent. Iran's reported instruction to Houthis to prepare Red Sea disruption if the US strikes Iranian power infrastructure introduces a further tail risk: simultaneous closure of both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb would materially tighten LNG supply into Europe, with direct upward pressure on both gas-fired generation costs and, indirectly, EUA prices as fuel switching increases coal burn. Data for this sector is thin beyond these macro linkages.
drivers: TTF at €56.31/MWh (+35% one month) is the primary upward cost pressure on gas-fired European power generation
EUA carbon market muted despite energy price volatility, implying limited fuel-switching or demand destruction signal priced in yet
Iran-Houthi threat to Bab el-Mandeb represents a key tail risk: dual chokepoint closure could sharply tighten European LNG supply and lift EUAs
